question:
The numbers, in order, of each row and the numbers, in order, of each column of a \(5\times5\) array of integers form an arithmetic progression of length \(5.\) The numbers in positions \((5,5),\) \((2,4),\) \((4,3),\) and \((3,1)\) are \(0,\) \(48,\) \(16,\) and \(12,\) respectively. What number is in position \((1,2)?\)

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \cdot & ? & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 48 & \cdot \\ 12 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & 16 & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
solution:
Equal spacing in an arithmetic progression lets us interpolate between known entries. Let \(a_{ij}\) denote the entry in row \(i\), column \(j\), and set \(a_{54}=d\). Since \(a_{55}=0\), row 5 must be
\[
4d,\ 3d,\ 2d,\ d,\ 0.
\]
In column 1, row 4 is midway between rows 3 and 5, so
\[
a_{41}=\frac{a_{31}+a_{51}}2
=\frac{12+4d}{2}=6+2d.
\]
In column 4, moving from row 2 to row 5 takes three equal steps. Row 4 is two of those steps from row 2, giving
\[
a_{44}=48+\frac23(d-48)=16+\frac{2d}{3}.
\]
Similarly, in row 4, column 3 is two of the three steps from column 1 to column 4. Hence
\[
16=a_{43}=\frac{a_{41}+2a_{44}}3
=\frac{6+2d+2(16+2d/3)}3.
\]
Multiplying by \(3\) and simplifying gives
\[
48=38+\frac{10d}{3},
\qquad d=3.
\]

Now \(a_{51}=4d=12\). Since \(a_{31}=12\) as well, column 1 has common difference zero, so \(a_{11}=12\). Also, \(a_{53}=2d=6\) and \(a_{43}=16\). Thus moving upward in column 3 adds \(10\) per row, and
\[
a_{13}=16+3\cdot10=46.
\]
Finally, \(a_{12}\) is the arithmetic mean of \(a_{11}\) and \(a_{13}\):
\[
a_{12}=\frac{12+46}{2}=\boxed{29}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
